#10559. Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist

A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.

Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.

The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.

A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision

Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.

To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.

"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."

The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.

Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.

A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare

To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.

When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.

The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.

The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.

"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."

The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.

Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough

The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.

Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.

The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.

"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."

Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.

Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices

The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.

In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.

Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.

"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."

As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

#10557. Apple is slashing AI budgets—the latest company to do so

Tokenmaxxing is on the way out, even as some of the biggest players in the tech industry are urging their employees to use AI as much as possible. A new Bloomberg report reveals that Apple is cutting employee budgets for AI token usage while remaining just as committed to deploying AI to boost efficiency. 

Apple has already reduced the daily spending limit from $300 to $200 for certain engineers, according to Bloomberg, but the company reportedly plans to cut that down even more. Sources told Bloomberg that the daily cap could drop as low as $100 for some engineering teams. In many other departments, daily AI spending is already capped at $100; now Apple is considering reducing the limit to $25 for certain teams. 

The spending limit is measured in tokens, which are units of AI usage that represent fragments of text or data processed by AI systems. 

This move comes as Apple continues pressing its engineers and other employees to use AI more in day-to-day operations. But it also reflects a larger trend rippling across the tech industry, as companies struggle to justify their outsize spending on artificial intelligence. 

After pushing their employees to adopt AI, many tech employers seem to be grappling with the fact that those investments have not yielded the productivity gains that they anticipated. 

According to Bloomberg, some Apple employees believed many people weren’t making use of the $300 limit and that it was higher than needed. But other employees seemed to view it as a sign that Apple is looking to reduce costs—and that the company could resort to layoffs. 

Bloomberg reports that Apple is already taking steps to streamline its operations in the interest of maximizing efficiency, and recently appointed CEO John Ternus is reportedly already advocating for reducing layers of management (something that Amazon has also sought to do over the last year).

There are plenty of signs tech companies are tightening their belts, even as they continue to prioritize AI adoption across their workforce. Uber exhausted its annual AI budget in a matter of months, leading the company to cap monthly spending at $1,500 for each AI coding tool. Companies like Meta, Microsoft, and Tesla have all imposed token limits on their employees. 

Beyond AI spend, however, the fear of layoffs looms large across the tech industry. 

A steady stream of employers have trimmed head count in the last year due to AI investments, either to offset exorbitant AI spending or because AI has enabled them to cut back on certain jobs. A number of companies, including Microsoft, have given their workers the option of taking a voluntary buyout, presumably to stave off job losses or avoid the negative attention associated with major layoffs. 

As Fast Company reported this week, some workers have even started to worry about AI being used to select employees for layoffs as companies shed jobs and reshape their workforce. In other words, it seems companies are continuing to demand more of their employees, but with less support—human or otherwise.

#10555. Will Galaxy S27 Ultra and Pixel 12 mark the end of the flagship era of smartphones?

Like most Android fans, you probably enjoy having the latest and greatest smartphone buried in your pocket. The best camera, the best display, the fastest processor, and of course, as much RAM as any given smartphone OEM will pack in. And even as we’ve watched the typical flagship price balloon into the four-digit space, trade-in offers, carrier deals, and steep sales on certain hardware brands like Pixel have made it all too easy to keep up on what’s new in gadgets without breaking the bank year-in and year-out.

Obviously, all of those routes towards a cheaper smartphone purchase still exist today — I assure you, anyone who regularly tunes into the NFL can recite Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T’s various deals by heart. But prices are rising so rapidly, with no sign of slowdown in sight, that I can no longer be sure any of those routes towards making new hardware more expensive will be available tomorrow. And honestly, we might hit a point where it’s increasingly difficult to recommend these phones to all but the most hardcore of enthusiasts, no matter how many sweeteners you add to the deal.

Throughout 2026, we’ve watched as new generations of barely-modified hardware have launched with $100 price hikes. We’ve watched as months-old hardware suddenly jumped up in price without so much in the way of a warning or an official announcement. And even outside of smartphones, you have to wonder if Google really hoped its latest lineup of laptops would’ve launched with more models available for under four figures. What’s been an underlying problem throughout the market throughout the last year, though, seems ready to burst into something much larger beginning throughout the next few months.

Recent price leaks have not exactly filled me with confidence over what hardware to recommend to anyone in the market for a new phone. The Galaxy S27 Ultra is sounding like it could arrive starting at $1,500, $100 more than the S26 Ultra’s current MSRP and $200 more than what that phone launched at earlier this year. Motorola’s attempt to come back to the flagship space in the US for the first time since 2023 could be completely derailed by rumors of an even higher price point that guarantees it won’t appeal to anyone. And while we’re certainly too far out to really predict anything regarding Google’s next-gen Pixel pricing, if you think the Pixel 12 might be your next phone, I’d start saving today.

As you climb towards the $2,000 mark, it’s worth putting these costs into perspective. These are laptop prices — maybe not that new “PROLED” MacBook Pro, but certainly other upper-high end laptops from companies like Apple, Dell, and HP. $1,500 will buy you an mid-tier home treadmill, or a nice OLED TV, to say nothing of the truly practical ways you can put that much cash to good use in a time where the costs of everything is rising. While some might think there is no price ceiling that truly keeps them away from new Android hardware, I’d be willing to bet plenty of potential buyers are already being priced out of the high-end market entirely. We’re reaching a breaking point where the question might not even be about whether you can afford something, but whether you should, leaving customers with just two routes forward: keep your existing device, or opt for a midrange option when you can.

Sure, saying “no thanks” to something like the Pixel 11 Pro XL right now might be easy enough. But moving forward, practically every single Android user will need to set some kind of personal limit on the price of a new smartphone, and if you’re convinced the midrange space might serve as your sole savior, you might want to think again. While RAM prices are bound to affect the final cost of Google’s Pixel 12, those constraints on a final bill of materials might mean a whole lot more to something like the Pixel 11a. After all, when you’ve already seen the Pixel 10a and its generation-old Tensor G4 chipset get hit with a $100 price bump, you have to wonder if it’s time to cut back on certain “premium” features.

The next few years of budget-oriented smartphones — and I really am talking about anything outside of the flagship space — is about to shift in a way we haven’t seen in over a decade. In the 2010s, cheap components and streamlined production costs helped bring about excellent midrange options like Google’s Pixel A-series, Samsung’s Galaxy A-series, and some select Moto G entries. Moving forward, these same companies will need to pick between higher prices and reduced spec sheets. The dream of yesterday’s flagship becoming tomorrow’s budget phone is, at least for the time being, dead and buried.

This isn’t just rampant speculation on my part. We’re already hearing about some companies making the decision to reduce RAM in their devices down to 8GB, 6GB, or even as low as 4GB, depending on the model and market it’s entering. It’s easy to see storage options also getting hit with their own downgrade — 128GB entry-level flagships could reemerge just as soon as they began to die off, and I wouldn’t be surprised to see 64GB options begin to reappear in sub-$600 models. That might be the sacrifice needed to keep other high-end features, like 120Hz OLED displays, hanging around in this price range.

I think after rebates, credits to Google One and AI Pro, my Pixel 11 Pro 512GB came out to ~$350, which would be amongst the smallest of all my "entertainment" expenses, and this is a tool I use multiple times a day that saves me time and money, also. I don't mind spending that money, and I don't see that stopping anytime soon. The only real issue is I wanted 16G of RAM on my device, and for that I spent more than I was expecting, but I'm pretty sure next year's trade-in will cover the additional expense.

I choose Pixel for the rapid updates, and Android, primarily. I can't get that with any other manufacturer except maybe sometimes Samsung.

I recognize I'm an outlier, my partner still runs a OnePlus 12r and is quite happy with it, and doesn't ever consider new phones unless it breaks.

If AI isn't making Google the money it needs for its stock to stay upwards, eventually things will need to change. Either phone prices/RAM comes down, or AI provides such a great life-changing experience (so far it definitely hasn't,) that I put my money elsewhere.

Of course, you can’t simply opt to forego RAM or storage in the same way that you can downgrade the display, and with the memory crunch set to possibly extend to 2030 or beyond, there could come a time where cutting back on raw specs or non-essential features stops being an either-or question. The knock-on effect is obvious: If you suddenly have a lot more people buying devices with less horsepower than previous generations, you’re going to see a reciprocal slowdown of any software development that requires hardware capable of reaching a certain threshold. Widespread on-device AI, for those of you who care about local models, seems like a pipedream at this point, but these market conditions are just as likely to crush, say, any hope of more games with high-end graphics coming to Android.

It’s not that the hardware won’t exist to support these features — flagships will obviously still exist even if their price tags balloon over the $2,000 mark. It’s the audience size you have to worry about; for a large majority of developers, it simply won’t make sense to continue pushing the envelope for what constitutes a smaller and smaller crowd of potential users.

The other solution is to hold onto whatever device you have in your possession right now, for as long as you can. That might not sound particularly exciting — I know I couldn’t tell you the last time I went more than six months without changing phones, even discounting review units — but it’s also the most reasonable approach to the current crisis. It’s not too late to jump on a recent flagship (think 2024 or later) before things get particularly dire, either, and with holiday sales coming up, I’d urge anyone on the fence about upgrading their current device with the means to do so to pull the trigger. Tomorrow’s price, simply put, will not be today’s.

And hey, if there’s a silver lining to be found here, I think it’s this: we’ve seeing tech companies across the board — hardware and software alike — grow increasingly comfortable with the idea that, for the user, resources can be effectively unlimited. Those days are gone, and it’s going to force software developers, including Google, to make some changes that are probably long, long overdue. We might lose out on big hardware improvements, resource-heavy advancements, and flagship-esque affordable smartphones, but there’s always a chance Chrome’s memory usage finally gets under control. It might not be worth all of this pain, but it’s something, right?

#10554. The midterm elections’ blue wave could throw a wrench in SpaceX’s mobile ambitions

Elon Musk has made no secret of his hopes of turning SpaceX into a viable competitor to mobile companies like Verizon and AT&T. But with the Democrats’ resounding victory in the 2026 midterm elections, that plan is suddenly thrown into question.

SpaceX has been busy over the past month making deals and positioning itself to step into the mobile space. In October, it bought an 800 MHz spectrum portfolio from private equity firm Grain Management, which had acquired it from T-Mobile following its 2020 merger with Sprint. And earlier this week, SpaceX struck a deal with Qualcomm to build out base stations for its planned mobile carrier. Taken together, those moves bring the company closer to entering the market.

But to launch the new division, SpaceX will also have to jump through legislative hoops, something that could be significantly more challenging with the Democrats in charge.

Several Democratic candidates made it clear they planned to target Musk—who spent $500 million trying to stop the blue wave—should the party gain a majority in the midterms.

Some lawmakers want to explore potential conflicts of interest in the billions of dollars Musk’s companies receive in federal contracts and subsidies. Others have questions about his possible role in throttling internet access to Ukraine’s army. And several want to do a deep dive into Musk’s role at DOGE (the Department of Government Efficiency that he spearheaded)—which accessed tremendous amounts of sensitive data.

Last December, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Democratic Representative Greg Casar of Texas began warning about SpaceX’s possible entry into the mobile market amid a proposed deal to acquire some wireless spectrum licenses from EchoStar.

That deal, they wrote at the time, “would help Musk expand SpaceX’s Starlink capacity and provide an opportunity for the company to gain ‘firepower’ in the satellite communications industry that competitors will struggle to compete with. . . . The close relationship of Mr. Musk to the Trump administration and to key Trump administration officials make it particularly important that the FCC and DOJ engage in a robust, independent, and impartial review.”

The deal, valued at $17 billion, ultimately went through.

Building a network

SpaceX didn’t stop there. Last month’s purchase of the 800 MHz spectrum portfolio seemed mundane at first glance. That frequency was used by Sprint to power its push-to-talk/walkie-talkie-like features in 2004. SpaceX, though, saw it as a way to bypass building an expensive, complex network of repeaters across the U.S. and the globe, when used in conjunction with its Starlink satellites.

“Starlink’s satellite signal at 2 GHz can reach your phone outdoors, but it dies at the first wall,” wrote Aakash Gupta, a product management leader, creator, and educator in a post on X. “800 MHz penetrates buildings. Most phones already have the band built in. So satellites handle the open sky, this low-band layer handles indoors, and suddenly Starlink Mobile covers everywhere a normal carrier does without the tower network.”

Musk was similarly upbeat, writing on X that the portfolio is “the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America.”

The deal with Qualcomm will enhance the cellular infrastructure and enable high-capacity coverage for Starlink Mobile. There are even reports SpaceX is in talks to buy Boost Mobile or use its network, which would give Musk another entry into the mobile market.

Allies and advantages

Come January, Musk will have significantly fewer friends on Capitol Hill—and many more enemies.

“We must get big money out of our politics, so no billionaire or trillionaire can buy our elections,” James Talarico, the Democratic Senator-elect from Texas, said in his victory speech. “We must unrig this economic system that only benefits the top 1%.”

Musk does have one powerful card up his sleeve, however. His relationship with President Donald Trump, which has been rocky in the past, is on solid footing once more, and Trump still controls executive agencies, including the Federal Communications Commission, which could help SpaceX’s entry into the market.

Timing could also play to Musk’s advantage. Verizon’s CEO has estimated it will take at least four years for SpaceX to become a viable player in the market. Musk claimed it would take half that time, but it’s worth remembering he has a history of being overly optimistic in his timeline forecasts.

Whether it’s two years, four years, or more, the past few elections have shown that, politically, a lot can change in that span.

#10551. Inside the jagged era of AGI: 5 key takeaways

Below, Kevin Roose shares five key insights from his new book, The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence.

Roose is an award-winning technology journalist, bestselling author, and cofounder of Machine Gods Media. He previously spent a decade as a technology columnist for The New York Times, where he co-created and cohosted the popular podcast Hard Fork. He now cohosts Machine Gods, an AI-focused podcast produced in partnership with NPR.

What’s the Big Idea?

For years, the world’s leading AI researchers have raced to build a technology that many of them fear. But the finish line keeps moving as AI becomes more capable. The truth is, we’re already living in the early, imperfect years of artificial general intelligence, and our institutions are dangerously unprepared for what comes next.

Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Roose himself—in the Next Big Idea app, or buy the book.

1. The people most afraid of AI are the ones building it.

This is, in some sense, the founding paradox of the whole AGI story. You’d assume the people building AI are true believers who expect it will do amazing things, like cure cancer and end poverty. And some of them are. But a surprising number of key figures in this race got into AI because they were terrified. They read the arguments about what a superintelligent machine might do to humanity, took them seriously, and concluded that if this thing was going to be built no matter what, it had better be built by people who were scared of it and would take the appropriate precautions.

Ultimately, I came to think of the AI world as having three tribes. There are the scientists, who see AGI as the ultimate intellectual challenge and want to use it to discover new drugs and cure disease. There are the seekers, who see it as an evolutionary turning point for our species. And then there are the survivalists, who think that if this technology isn’t built by the good guys, then the bad guys will do it instead.

The trouble is that getting there first is what everyone is trying to do. And they all end up concluding that the only way to move forward responsibly is to accelerate. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, left OpenAI partly out of concern that it was moving too fast, and then went on to build a competitor that had to move just as fast to stay ahead. He’s living inside the paradox, and so are many of the people in this book.

2. The secret was a big blob of compute.

For most of AI’s history, smart people assumed building an intelligent machine would require understanding the human brain, writing down the rules of reasoning, and encoding knowledge the way you teach a student. But what worked instead was almost embarrassingly simple.

Amodei outlined it in a 2017 paper he called “Big Blob of Compute.” Essentially, you take a neural network, feed it enormous amounts of data, and then throw a huge computer at it. The model then learns to recognize the patterns in that data the same way a human toddler does, by looking at a lot of examples until it clicks.

Amodei called this his Big Blob of Compute hypothesis, and it reoriented OpenAI’s research away from narrow applications and toward a more general approach. It’s what led to GPT-1, GPT-2, and ultimately to the large language models that we use today. This simple recipe is the engine of everything that follows.

3. Feeling the AGI is a key ingredient in AI progress.

In San Francisco, people talk about “feeling the AGI” as a kind of spiritual awakening that comes from living on the technological frontier, internalizing the enormously fast pace of progress, and building up to something unimaginably vast. The people who work at these companies believe that they are building something closer to an alien species than a product, and they treat their work as a humanitarian mission: deliver AGI safely into the world before someone else screws it up.

“Feeling the AGI” is what Ilya Sutskever, the former chief scientist of OpenAI, called this feeling. He’d stand up at company gatherings and lead chants. He burned effigies. “Don’t lose sight of what we’re actually building here,” he said. “This is not a tool. This is something more like a being.”

Feeling the AGI is now pretty common. It’s why we see researchers from AI companies speaking up about their fears and why lawmakers and regulators are desperate to slow down this industry. But for many years, the people feeling the AGI were few and far between. They worked at a handful of small AI companies that were little known to the general public. And they shared this secret which led them to double down on their research. The people who felt the AGI early won. They became the people who now run some of the most powerful companies on Earth.

4. There is no finish line.

For years, everyone in the race to AGI operated under the unspoken assumption that the race would eventually end. The idea was that someone would train an AI model that was clearly as smart as the smartest humans. That person would walk out on a stage and say, “We have built AGI!” And the race would be over.

Some leaders even started making plans for after AGI. Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, mused about handing over control of the company to an AGI and finding some hobbies for himself. Demis Hassabis, former CEO of DeepMind Technologies, told friends he would take a yearlong sabbatical and wander the gardens in Princeton, New Jersey, the way Albert Einstein did. Dario Amodei wanted to spend more time at his family’s farm in Italy with his favorite horse, Calypso.

But around 2025, I started hearing a different phrase in AI circles. They called this the Red Queen’s race. It comes from evolutionary biology, via Lewis Carroll, where the Red Queen tells Alice that it takes all the running you can do just to stay in the same place. That’s what the race to AGI has become. Nobody agrees on what AGI is or how we’ll know that we’ve achieved it.

Every time one company ships a breakthrough, the others match it within months, and the goalposts get moved again. At Google, Larry Page, the cofounder who had been thinking about AGI longer than almost anyone, reportedly told people he would rather see Google go bankrupt than lose the race. Meanwhile, other Google executives were saying that AGI was still five years or more away. And the CEO, Sundar Pichai, was barely using the word at all.

Everyone in AI is running as fast as they can, and nobody is getting anywhere relative to each other. So unless this changes, or we slow the whole thing down, the post-AGI future of garden strolls and hobbies and Calypso the horse will have to wait.

5. AGI is here, whether we feel it or not.

By the definitions of AGI that people in 2016 were using—a machine that can do most cognitive tasks about as well as most humans—I think we’ve already gotten there. Today’s AI models can write, code, analyze documents, pass professional exams, solve unsolved math problems, and tutor children. If you went back in a time machine with a laptop and a copy of ChatGPT or Claude to 2017 or 2018 and showed them to a thousand of the leading researchers in the field, they would not have hesitated to say this is obviously AGI.

The reason that it doesn’t feel like AGI is that this intelligence is jagged. AI systems are superhuman at some things and bafflingly bad at others. They can solve the Riemann hypothesis or disprove the Jacobian conjecture and then miscount the letters in a word or fail at basic arithmetic. That unevenness makes it easy to dismiss them. You just find the one thing they can’t do and conclude that it’s all hype.

But a jagged intelligence is still an intelligence. In some ways, our human intelligence is just as jagged. I’ve come to think that the useful definition of AGI isn’t about capability. It’s about generality: a single system that can be pointed at almost any problem and make real progress on it. By that standard, we’re not waiting for AGI to arrive. We’re living in the early, awkward, jagged years of it.

One of the biggest risks I see isn’t a robot uprising. It’s a world where the technology has already changed, and the institutions in charge of our society—governments, companies, schools, and communities—keep acting like it hasn’t. The people in this book have been feeling the AGI for years. Now it’s time for the rest of us to catch up.

This article originally appeared in Next Big Idea Club magazine and is reprinted with permission.

Following a month of beta testing, Apple Music 7.0 is rolling out with a Liquid Glass redesign for Android, as well as the new icon for the streaming service.

The app now has a floating bottom bar that lets you see content above, below, and to the sides. There is a small amount of translucency that primarily allows you to make out solid colors underneath the navigation element. Version 7.0 introduces a very modern, edge-to-edge design for Android’s system status and navigation bars.

Dear Apple, use Material 3 Expressive for your apps. Google has honored your design language by building their apps with Liquid Glass, now you need to return the favor and build with Google's design language

Top bars across Apple Music have been updated. The page title and overflow menu are now on the same line, while the three-dot icons are no longer themed red and have been placed in circular containers. The Library tab sees a big update with “Edit Pins” and “Edit Categories” now part of the three-dot menu.

Artist pages have been thoroughly redesigned with the background now themed based on the cover image. Matching the iOS design, there’s a prominent play button and info page, while share has been placed in the top-right corner.

The Settings page has also been modernized with better grouping. There are no major changes to Now Playing, which did not see any big updates on iOS.

#10548. Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10547. Amazon controls its delivery drivers. NYC wants it to employ them, too

Every workday, Luc Rene puts on a shirt and pants branded with Amazon’s logo and heads to a distribution center, where he climbs into a van that also carries Amazon’s logo across its side to deliver packages with the company’s swoosh smile emblazoned on them. When he rings customers’ doorbells, he yells out, “Amazon.”

But Rene is not technically an Amazon employee. He’s employed by a delivery service provider (DSP) that contracts out his labor.

That could soon change in New York City, where Rene lives and works, if the City Council passes the Delivery Protection Act. The bill would require companies like Amazon to directly employ the people who deliver their packages while also creating a licensing system that would hold the companies to new safety, training, and labor standards. It has the backing of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and 31 of the council’s 51 members—enough for it to pass if brought to a vote. Supporters of the bill say it would increase street safety while also providing better protection for the workers who deliver Amazon packages.

Amazon has lobbied heavily against the bill. “We’re committed to creating good jobs and supporting our thousands of employees in New York City. We’re equally committed to the local small-business partners who work with us every day to provide fast, reliable delivery for New Yorkers,” Amazon spokesperson Steve Kelly tells Fast Company. “But as written, this legislation would directly undermine that commitment—threatening the small businesses that deliver to customers, putting the jobs of more than 5,000 of their employees at risk, and forcing us to consider relocating delivery operations outside of the city.”

Safety on the job has been an issue for Rene ever since he started delivering Amazon packages in 2022. After completing a training on a computer, he was supposed to spend a day being trained by an experienced driver; the driver never showed up, so Rene drove by himself. Since he was never told how to avoid injury during his shifts, which stretch 10 or more hours, he’s come up with his own regimen, stretching before and after work.

“No driver is ever required to complete a delivery if conditions aren’t safe—and neither they nor their DSP is penalized for making that call,” Amazon’s Kelly says. “Any allegation of unsafe working conditions would be taken seriously and we investigate accordingly.”

In 2023, Rene slipped and injured his knees while delivering a package. Unsure whether he could access Amazon’s medical services, he called his employer, which asked only whether he could keep working. He did, despite the pain, taking painkillers to get through it. “If I can’t show up to work due to the pain, I won’t get paid,” he says.

His experience appears to be common: A 2025 report from the New York City comptroller’s office found that last-mile facilities like the DSP that employs Rene reported an average of 678 injuries per year from 2022 to 2024, and 85% of them were severe enough to keep people from working or to need a reassignment. Amazon’s DSP program had the highest injury rates.

In response to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the New York Delivers coalition, which represents DSPs and is bankrolled by $5 million in money from Amazon, says DSPs “provide flexible, good-paying jobs with strong workplace standards, opportunities for career advancement, and competitive benefits,” adding that the Delivery Protection Act “effectively eliminates the small businesses in the industry, and puts over 10,000 New York City jobs at risk.” Amazon also paid to bus in workers and DSP owners to oppose the bill in a city council hearing earlier this year.

“On paper, Amazon’s not my employer”

When Rene started driving, all he and his fellow drivers were given to haul packages, some of which weigh more than 40 pounds, were giant plastic bins called totes. He says it took a strike in 2024 and a march on their boss to get hand trucks. The effort of dragging totes across the ground left Rene with back pain that lingers today.

There are other health and safety issues. In the summer, the heat is “really painful,” he says. But two years ago, Amazon instituted a change that means when he exits his van, the air-conditioning shuts off, leaving the van to bake while he makes his deliveries. The DSP has no control over that, he says, nor over how many packages he’s expected to deliver in such conditions.

In fact, Amazon directly controls much of Rene’s workday. When he shows up to the DSP, he has to hope Amazon provided enough routes for him to actually work that day; otherwise, he gets sent home. He must be in full company uniform before even leaving the dispatch center to get in his van. Once he arrives at the van, he has to go through an inspection checklist created by Amazon before he can drive the vehicle. If a defect is found, it’s Amazon that decides to ground the van, and the DSP has no power to override the decision, Rene says.

Further, Rene says Amazon dictates how much time he gets to load up the van before facing a penalty. Kelly denies that Amazon controls workers’ schedules, saying, however, that it does “assign dispatch windows.”

Cameras inside the delivery van watch Rene’s every move during his shift—and it’s Amazon, not the DSP, that watches the feed. (Kelly asserts that the cameras are only for safety and not for productivity or performance tracking, although many reports have disputed that.) If Rene presses the accelerator or hits the breaks too hard, Amazon gives him an infraction. If he gets into an accident while driving a delivery van and calls the DSP, he’ll be forwarded to an Amazon representative.

“On paper, Amazon’s not my employer, but in reality, Amazon is,” he says.

For all of this, Rene makes $25 an hour—a figure he arrived at only after a recent 25-cent raise that was implemented by Amazon. If the Delivery Protection Act passes, it “would change everything, honestly,” Rene says. Although he’s a member of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters union, the act would allow him and his fellow delivery drivers not only to unionize but also to negotiate directly with Amazon.

Then they can demand better training, higher pay, health insurance (especially critical for workers injured on the job), more control over their schedules, and a guaranteed 40-hour workweek. “All those little things to make the job feel, not easy, but basically like I can show up to work today and I know I’m safe,” he says. “Make it feel like I have something reliable, something people can actually live on.”

#10545. AI, DevOps and the Cost of Hosting: From Idea to Production for $0

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An AI coding agent rebuilt my photo-collage app as a distributed system and deployed it to a free server. The hard part turned out to be hardware: one free ARM CPU, 538 collages created during load testing, zero failed jobs, and $0 a month.

Like most developers, I have never been short of product ideas. Hosting them has always been the problem. I have tried shared hosting with SmartWeb, Azure free credits, Google Compute Engine’s free VM instances, SmartWeb’s virtual private servers, and Heroku dynos. None of them left me satisfied. The worst experience was a $200 charge for an AI address API on Google Cloud—for an application that never earned me a single kobo.

I am not a cheapskate, but I learned quickly that one of the easiest ways to kill a potentially good idea is to get the finances wrong. An application has to stay online until it reaches a critical mass of users, and hosting an untested, unverified product on expensive hardware can be wasteful.

Agentic AI coding has changed how quickly I can move from idea to production. Over about five weeks of intermittent coding—amounting to roughly three days of full work with Claude—my photo-stitching app went from an Angular 8 project that would not even build to a distributed system running in production.

Along the way, Claude upgraded the front end from Angular 8 to Angular 22 and fixed the build on Node 24. It set up RabbitMQ with Docker Compose so the message broker configures itself on startup, and added real-time notifications over SignalR with a progress spinner. It fixed a crash loop caused by an unreadable iPhone photo. It redesigned the system so any server can process any job, with switchable database and file storage, direct browser-to-storage uploads, and photos resized in the browser before upload. It added reliability work that a team might debate for a sprint: a dead-letter queue, confirmed publishing, idempotent workers, recovery of stuck jobs, and automatic clean-up. It fixed the stitching so photos keep their proportions and borders are even. It wrote 41 automated tests and scrubbed leaked passwords and personal photos from the Git history.

Coding, QA, DevOps, and production support used to be separate phases, often handled by separate people. Here they happened in one conversation. When code becomes this cheap to produce, the bottleneck moves. For me, it moved to hardware.

To check what the AI builds, you have to run it locally. A distributed app means running the whole system locally: a web app, a background worker, a message broker, a database, and storage emulators. Because Claude adds features quickly, and each one can add another container, it is easy to exhaust a laptop’s RAM and CPU.

My setup made this lesson concrete. I work on a MacBook Air, with Visual Studio in a Windows virtual machine. Docker cannot run inside that VM on Apple Silicon, so Claude ran Docker on the Mac and drove it from Windows over SSH. Later, my mobile connection started dropping large packets and broke uploads from the VM, so Claude moved the load testing onto the server itself. The software problems took minutes. The hardware and network problems took longer.

Then comes hosting. Heroku looked like the easy route, but it has had no free dynos since 2022. The cheapest option is an Eco dyno at about $5 a month, plus about $5 for Postgres. That is affordable, but running it for an idea that has no users yet did not seem prudent.

Claude suggested Oracle Cloud’s Always Free tier: an ARM server with up to 4 CPUs and 24 GB of RAM, free with no end date. I created a small instance with 1 CPU and about 6 GB. Claude wrote a production Docker Compose file and a one-command setup script: Caddy as the gateway, the web app, the stitching worker, RabbitMQ, and PostgreSQL, with data that survives restarts. My repository is private, so rather than put a GitHub token on a public server, it copied the code over SSH and deployed it. The last blocker was mine to fix: opening ports 80 and 443 in Oracle’s network firewall. Then the site was live.

I did not want to guess, so I asked Claude to load-test the live server. Simulated users ran the full flow: upload two photos, wait for the real-time notification, and download the stitched collage.

The server handled 64 people creating collages at the same moment without a single failed job: 538 collages, zero errors. Its ceiling was about 62 collages a minute—one per second. Beyond that, users queue. With 4 people creating at once, 95% of collages arrived within about five seconds; at 64, each person waited about a minute. If each active user makes a collage every couple of minutes, one CPU comfortably serves around 85 people at once, and a few hundred if they use it less often.

The test also showed what runs out first, and it is not the CPU. Each collage stores about 5 MB, mostly the PNG output, so at full speed the disk would fill in under two hours. Switching to JPEG and shortening retention fixes that, and when traffic grows, three more free CPUs are waiting. That is the value of measuring before paying: I know what to change, and when.

Oracle isn’t being charitable. Servers need applications to run—ideally ones that go viral—and the free tier is a play for loyalty. Oracle wants successful projects to stay and grow into its paid services instead of moving off the platform once they reach critical mass. It can also reclaim free instances that sit idle.

I think the bet is smart, and it points to a bigger trend. AI-generated code still needs energy to run and hardware to host it, even when far fewer people work on each project. As more people turn ideas into working software, demand for compute will keep growing, and I expect hosting and data centres to become a very profitable business.

For now, the combination works: Claude orchestrates the coding, QA, and DevOps, and Oracle’s free server keeps an idea online long enough to find out whether it deserves to grow.

#10543. Give your products an annual review

I spent the first half of my career as the product manager at a software company. Product teams are constantly reviewing their products, assessing: What do our customers want? What changes should we make? Do we (maybe) need to retire a product altogether because it no longer serves its purpose?

Most solopreneurs don’t take the same approach. They continue to push the same products or services, or tack on new items until they have a large suite of offers they have to maintain. We rarely take anything away.

I’ve gotten into the habit of an annual review to make sure everything I put out into the world for my business still makes sense for both me and my customers. 

The trap of adding and never subtracting

Part of the joy of running a solo business is launching something new. You get to make all the decisions about what an offer looks like and how to launch it. 

Removing an offer is a lot less fun. It can feel like a loss. Plus, you may have material (website, slide decks, email sequences) that need to be updated.

The problem is that every offer needs upkeep. Content gets out of date. You may also be paying for tools related to hosting or delivering an offer that isn’t doing anything for you. 

I create a lot of resources for solopreneurs, often describing systems or processes that make a solo business run efficiently. These can quickly feel dated—or even obsolete—as technology changes. 

For a long time, I spent my precious hours creating new resources without a process for updating existing material. That’s a mistake, since outdated information quickly erodes trust.

The questions I ask about every offer

Now I take time to review every product and service I offer and ask myself the same questions:

Is anyone buying it? I start with sales or bookings from the past year. Low numbers aren’t automatically a reason to cut, but I need to review the offer more closely.

Do I still want to do this work? A service can sell well and still be work you don’t enjoy.

What does it cost me to maintain? I count the time I spend updating information and supporting it, plus the time it takes to promote. Then I add any tool subscriptions tied to it.

Does it still fit where my business is headed? An offer that made sense two years ago may not match the clients or work I want now. 

I maintain a business road map and value statements, and compare my offers against these documents. I use AI to help this process by having Claude do the initial comparison. This becomes my checklist for a human review and assessment.

What to do with an offer that isn’t working

Keeping an offer as is and cutting it aren’t the only two choices. There are a few other paths:

  • Refresh it: Update outdated content.
  • Reprice or repackage it: Raise the price or bundle it with something else so it doesn’t stand on its own.
  • Re-promote it: Sometimes there’s nothing wrong with the offer; perhaps it just hasn’t been marketed enough.
  • Retire it: Take it down, and let existing customers or clients know if needed.

I have a resource related to AI tools for solopreneurs. It made sense when I first created it several years ago. Now it’s impossible to maintain because the AI changes at lightning speed. Instead of spending my time updating it, I spent my time finding all the places where I reference this resource and removing it.

But to start, the most important step is making the time for a review. Block off time on your calendar once a year or put it on your to-do list. The review process is separate from acting on your decision. Your goal is to land on “Where do I go from here?”

#10540. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

#10538. How the country’s tallest mural was painted onto the side of this NYC building

In the South Bronx, residents can now look up to their heritage—literally.

A new mural by the Dominican artist Néstor Omar García, who also goes by the name Angurria, climbs 29 stories high on one tower in the Morrisania Air Rights public housing campus. It fills the skyline with a colorful take on a neighborhood block party crowded with children, elders, and, yes, even a DJ.

Titled Un MAR de Gente / From Every Shore, the artwork is said to be the tallest mural in the U.S., transforming an otherwise dull concrete facade of the brutalist New York City Housing Authority building into a public artwork.

The project was spearheaded by the New York City-based nonprofit ArtBridge and the strategic consulting firm FOGA. Support came in the form of grants from Public Housing Community Fund and MAC Viva Glam, the line of lipsticks that helps fund community causes. For a little over a year, the organizers worked alongside the artist and the community to complete the artwork.

“Hundreds of windows face this wall—neighbors, schools, offices—so everyone can enjoy this mural from their windows,” says FOGA’s founder, Fernando Ortiz.

Stacked into three sections that blend into one another, the mural collages three interconnected stories into a single scene. The top section symbolizes how older generations pass down knowledge to younger ones. To depict this, Angurria painted his “Doña Patria” character—a woman wearing hair rollers that he based on his mother and frequently returns to in his work—carrying a child on her shoulders.

The middle section features a party scene, with seven people wearing common emblems and fashion from the neighborhood. One dons the borough’s “X” symbol on a hat while an elder with a beard sports a Knicks cap and an orange tracksuit. In the corner, a young woman wears a hijab and Yankees jersey.

The bottom section shows two children playing around an open fire hydrant, which represents the past and the innocence of childhood.

The entire artwork was conceived of collaboratively with the community. FOGA organized six workshops with South Bronx residents to gain their input. Together they voted on artist they wanted to make the mural, the bright color palette, and the symbols and motifs that would be depicted, like hip-hop and sports teams.

After deciding on the mural’s nonnegotiables, the group passed the list to Angurria, who would then return with design concepts. They traded ideas and feedback until they were all happy with the result.

The mural is 307 feet tall, and the scale serves a purpose. “We look down at our phones so much and public art forces you to look up,” Jon Souza, program director at ArtBridge, tells Fast Company. Like the mural’s main figure who is looking upward, Doña Patria, passersby need to look up from their phones and up to the sky to view the whole work.

“You can’t experience the mural without doing the same,” Souza said.

Installing a mural at the scale of a 29-story building involved careful logistical planning. Just three artists painted it.

Many murals are first traced using a projection, but due to the size of the wall, that was not possible here. So Angurria turned to virtual reality (VR) instead. Using measurements from the building’s blueprints, he mapped out the final design to scale and divided it into sections, assigning a corresponding pattern to each floor.

Angurria and an additional artist then jumped on a swing scaffolding lift—the kind window washers use—and traced the virtual pattern, visible through the VR headset, onto the facade. Just laying down the figures’ black outline took around one full day. Next, they applied acrylic paint, then latex; they finished the details with spray paint. The entire process took 22 days.

The mural has become a conversation piece. Community members who contributed to the project proudly point out how their ideas are now part of the cityscape. That, more than the mural’s monumental size, is the greatest outcome as far as the organizers are concerned.

“We set out to create the mural without knowing the record-breaking scale it would ultimately reach,” Souza says. “But the scale, attention, and recognition it received have only amplified the sense of pride and ownership around the project.”

Angurria, though not part of the Bronx by birth, was embraced by the community as a result of the mural. On the artist’s birthday, which landed on one of the 22 days spent painting the piece, neighbors brought him cake and coffee.

“He is the artist who did the mural, but now he is also family,”  said Ortiz, the FOGA consultant.
